A review team has room to investigate only a small share of payments. This
example asks whether keeping individual transactions helps rank the payments
that will receive a dispute report, compared with a model using history
summaries.

::: {.callout-note title="Fictional benchmark"}
All data, schemas, and results on this page are fictional placeholders.
No benchmark has been run.
:::

## Example

One fictional labeled observation contains the transactions available at an
account-review cutoff:

```yaml
trxns:
  - booked_at: "2026-05-21T10:00:00"
    amount: 32.00
    merchant: Station Cafe
    hours_since_previous: null
    disputed: false
  - booked_at: "2026-05-27T18:15:00"
    amount: 56.20
    merchant: North Market
    hours_since_previous: 152.25
    disputed: true
  - booked_at: "2026-05-28T14:30:00"
    amount: 84.50
    merchant: North Market
    hours_since_previous: 20.25
    disputed: false
```

The common cutoff is May 28, 2026 at 14:30. Every `disputed` label means a new
dispute reported against that transaction during the following 30 days. The
answers are attached after the window has completed and hidden from all inputs.
The entire listed sequence is valid context at this shared cutoff; these are
not separate forecasts made at the earlier booking times.

`hours_since_previous` supplies elapsed time, while `DateParts` supplies
calendar cycles. The first gap is null because the first supplied transaction
has no predecessor in this observation. See [Preprocessing](../guides/preprocessors.qmd#derive-a-value)
for the derivation.

## Schema

```{typst}
//| label: fig-benchmark-payment-disputes
//| fig-cap: "Fictional schema: the same transaction sequence provides context and a hidden dispute target at every position."
//| fig-alt: "An account root owns one repeated trxns branch. Each transaction has DateParts booked_at, Number amount, Category merchant, Number hours_since_previous, and a Boolean disputed target hidden from input at every position."
#tree(node("account", kind: "root", body: [One review cutoff.], children: (
  node("trxns", kind: "branch", repeated: true, children: (
    node("booked_at", type: "DateParts", body: [Calendar cycles.]),
    node("amount", type: "Number"),
    node("merchant", type: "Category"),
    node("hours_since_previous", width: 180pt, type: "Number", body: [Elapsed hours; first gap null.]),
    node("disputed", kind: "target", type: "Boolean", body: [Hidden for every transaction.]),
  )),
)))
```

<details class="proof-details">
<summary>Complete model schema</summary>

```python
import relflow as rf

model = rf.Model.xs(
    trxns=rf.Branch(
        length=32,
        overflow="tail",
        booked_at=rf.DateParts(
            dateparts=["day_of_month", "day_of_week", "hour_of_day"],
        ),
        amount=rf.Number,
        merchant=rf.Category,
        hours_since_previous=rf.Number,
        disputed=rf.Boolean(mask=True),
    ),
)
```

The anonymous root contains only `trxns`; `account` is the diagram's descriptive
label. Input histories are oldest to newest, so the branch keeps the last 32
transactions. Prediction records omit `disputed` from every transaction and
retain the other fields. Results remain aligned at
`predictions.trxns[i].disputed`, with `inferred: true` at every retained position.

</details>

## Comparison

Compare gradient-boosted trees using each transaction's fields and account
history summaries with the sequence model above. The summaries include
transaction count, spend totals, amount ranges, merchant counts, and gap
statistics over the same retained history. Both models receive the same
cutoff-safe evidence and predict the same transaction labels.

Rank payments for a fixed review capacity. PR-AUC summarizes ranking across
thresholds; recall at a 5% review rate asks how many later disputes fall in the
highest-scoring 5% of transactions.

## Result

| Fictional model | PR-AUC ↑ | Recall at 5% review rate ↑ |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Trees with history summaries | 0.31 | 0.52 |
| RelFlow transaction sequence | 0.34 | 0.56 |

: Fictional placeholder results for the proposed comparison. {#tbl-benchmark-payment-disputes}

The example pairs overall ranking quality with capture at the team's review
budget. A measured comparison would also report uncertainty, calibration, and
the cost of preparing and scoring the history.

<details class="proof-details">
<summary>Fictional method, splits, and controls</summary>

### Cohort and outcome

The imaginary cohort contains accounts with at least one eligible payment and
one review snapshot per account. Each snapshot ends at its latest booking and
contains at most 32 transactions. All input values must have been available at
that cutoff. A dispute is a reported customer outcome, not automatically fraud.

Every retained transaction has a settled Boolean label for the same next
30-day window. Accounts whose outcome windows are incomplete are excluded from
the labeled cohort; an unobserved outcome is not converted to `false`.

### Proposed split

| Split | Fictional snapshot cutoffs |
| --- | --- |
| Train | January–August 2025 |
| Validation | October–November 2025 |
| Test | January–June 2026 |

Account groups are disjoint across splits. The intervening months separate
the 30-day label windows. Merchant vocabularies, numeric state, and application
summary statistics are learned only from training observations. Hyperparameters
and review policies are chosen on validation; test is reserved for the final
comparison.

These imaginary Parquet paths illustrate how already-prepared application
inputs would be connected. No such files are supplied by this page:

```python
data = rf.ArrowDataModule(
    model=model,
    train="fictional/payment-disputes/train.parquet",
    validate="fictional/payment-disputes/validation.parquet",
    test="fictional/payment-disputes/test.parquet",
)
```

### Controls for a real run

- Use the same accounts, retained transactions, label windows, and tuning budget
  for both models. Include a transaction-only baseline to isolate history's value.
- Calculate elapsed gaps before model binding. If histories are clipped first,
  calculate gaps after that clipping; later branch overflow does not recompute them.
- Score each retained transaction once. Calculate PR-AUC as average precision;
  rank within each review day's eligible pool for the 5% capacity metric.
- Repeat training seeds and estimate uncertainty by resampling accounts,
  preserving dependence among their transactions. Inspect calibration separately.

</details>
